Testing, correction and retesting

Unit 1 · Week 10 · Lesson 2 · Suggested 55-minute plan; adjust to local timing.

Prepare: Bring an integrated practice program, a disposable folder, synthetic test fixtures and workbook section 4. Preserve a clean starting copy for each destructive or failure test.

Suggested answers are teacher guidance, not extra assessment tasks. These notes are public.

1. Testing, correction and retesting

Suggested time: 2 minutes

Instructional strategy: Learning intention

Success means execute a requirement-linked test set, record expected and actual results honestly, isolate failures and verify repairs with regression checks. This is the existing project testing workshop, not an extra weighted test.

2. Retrieval: useful test evidence

Suggested time: 5 minutes

Instructional strategy: Individual retrieval and peer explanation

A desk-check predicts state; an executed test records actual behaviour. The expected result comes from the brief/independent calculation. A repair requires rerunning the failed case and earlier relevant cases. Distinguish unit tests of one module from integration tests of cooperating modules.

3. A test set follows requirements

Suggested time: 6 minutes

Instructional strategy: Test selection and prioritisation

Students assign IDs and precise expectations. R1 needs integer text conversion, range and retry cases, including zero. R2 ordinary/zero costs. R3 list order and zero retention. R4 separate records across two runs and a safe failure. R5 empty, single, several and tied maxima. This overview is not the complete test log. Ask for invalid ID cases: empty, comma and line break.

4. Boundary and recovery cases

Suggested time: 8 minutes

Instructional strategy: Guided prediction and partner challenge

For the non-negative integer quantity rule, -1 rejects, 0 accepts, 1 accepts. three and 2.5 reject as integer text. A retry sequence three,-1,0 should finish with accepted zero and no rejected values saved. Ask students to add a blank ID and a comma-containing ID test, with a later valid value. Define the response before executing.

5. Reproducing a failure

Suggested time: 7 minutes

Instructional strategy: Teacher think-aloud and minimal-case debugging

Use the chapter tie case [5,5] returning index 1 instead of 0. Reproduce with the smallest two-item fixture, trace remembered best index, identify >= versus >, then correct and rerun the tie case. Also rerun [2,0,5], a single item and empty. Students must identify the cause rather than changing several unrelated lines. The example is a debugging illustration, not claimed evidence about their own program.

6. Evidence workshop

Suggested time: 17 minutes

Instructional strategy: Independent testing with teacher conferences

Students execute their planned tests using resettable fixtures, log results, repair one priority fault and retest. Columns: test ID, requirement, setup/input, expected, actual, pass/fail, correction and retest evidence. Do not mark unexecuted cases as passed. Support: teacher models one record and provides a trace template. Extension: inject a known failure in a private copy to see whether the tests expose it. Use only disposable files for file-mode and failure trials.

7. An honest result record

Suggested time: 5 minutes

Instructional strategy: All-student hinge question

Correct B. The learner has only predicted or desk-checked, so the log should show planned/not executed. A screenshot of code is not evidence that the particular test ran. Discuss why an honest open failure is more informative than a false pass. Ask for the exact additional evidence needed to change the status.

8. Checkpoint: readiness for a user trial

Suggested time: 5 minutes

Instructional strategy: Independent readiness decision

Retain completed logs and explain whether the core workflow can be trialled safely. If core defects remain, specify them and fix before an unassisted trial, or clearly scope the trial and record the limitation. Do not invent successful results. Teacher checks that saved sample files use synthetic data and tests cover the agreed requirements.
